description: Hand-labelled semantic-retrieval set (the eval harness, crates/b2-embed/evals/). Each query avoids the target note's keywords (synonyms/paraphrase) so it measures semantic lift, not lexical overlap. `relevant` lists the vault-relative path(s) that should rank first. The corpus clusters notes into confusable topic groups (coffee, sleep, plants, security, geology, cycling), so ranking WITHIN a cluster is tested, not just across unrelated topics. An optional `passage` is a short verbatim phrase from the target passage: those queries are additionally scored at CHUNK level (does the ranked chunk's text contain the phrase?), which is what makes chunking changes visible to the eval (index-engine.md, GH #44). Keep passages verbatim, short, and unique within the corpus — and NOT identical to a heading, since `prepend_heading_path` injects the breadcrumb into chunk text and a heading-matching passage would then match for a reason unrelated to retrieval. The passage-labelled block added for #44 deliberately targets the three places chunking decides the outcome: content buried in a TABLE far from its heading, an UNLABELLED subsection, and a DEEP section a paraphrase alone must reach. The final four queries are the STEMMER-ADVERSARIAL block (GH #157), and they deliberately BREAK the avoid-the-target's-keywords rule: they measure lexical precision under tokenizer changes, not semantic lift. The universe/university pair shares a Porter stem (`univers`), so each query's target and its rival collide lexically under a stemmed tokenizer and not under unicode61 — a tokenizer A/B that improves recall elsewhere must not degrade these. The two git queries are code-literal: their passages are command text inside fenced code, where retrieval being LITERAL is the point. The final five queries are the NEGATIVE block (invariants.md D2, GH #201): an empty `relevant` means the labelled answer is NO MATCHES — the vault holds no evidence for the query, the query-side sibling of similar.json's negative anchors. Two are nonsense strings (the first is the dogfood report's literal query); three are real-language topics whose content tokens are audit-verified absent from the corpus, word-boundary and stem-prefix both (the audit rejected `teaching`/`training` for parrots — `teach`/`train` land in campus-life and running-and-aquarium — plus `castle` for chess's castling, `square` for its squares, `boat` for the knots note, `routine` for sleep-hygiene's bedtime routine, and `human` outright). Negative queries are excluded from every rank aggregate — adding one moves no pre-existing number — and are scored only by the search evidence calibration, which is also why they carry no `passage`. The optional `tail_relevant` key (GH #206) is the PER-HIT depth the per-rank tail rule is judged from: the notes BEYOND `relevant` that are honest evidence for the query — a reader with this information need, served one in the tail of the results, would not call the row filler, though it should never outrank the `relevant` note. The judgement is EXHAUSTIVE over the corpus for every positive query: a served note in neither `relevant` nor `tail_relevant` is irrelevant BY LABEL, not by omission — which is exactly the statement the old labels could not make, and the reason a tail rule could not be judged before this key existed. Encoded by NOTE, never by rank: per-rank relevance of any served list is derived (is the row's note in the keep-set?), so the labels stay true when the engine reorders — a per-query "last relevant rank" mark would freeze one ranking into the label file and make every legitimate reranking change a relabelling, the habit process rule 2 exists to prevent. Doubt breaks toward KEEPING (labelling tail-relevant): a wrongly-kept note only tightens the constraint on a tail rule, while a wrongly-omitted one would let a rule cut a real match and read clean — the same asymmetry that placed the query bar's constants toward the serving side. The deliberate judgement calls, both directions: the multi-topic notes are tail-relevant where one half bears (radio-and-sleep-debt's sleep-debt half for the two sleeplessness queries, pour-over-and-pottery's pour-over half for the immersion-brew and cup-taste queries, tire-pressure-and-knots' tire half for the hill-climb query, week-log's lava-field section for the volcano query); and same-cluster is NOT tail-relevance (dreaming is filler for the sleeplessness queries — REM imagery does not bear on falling asleep; espresso is filler for the french-press query; plant-roots and houseplant-care are filler for the photosynthesis-mechanism query; the universe/university stemmer pair is lexical by design and neither is evidence for the other). Negative queries carry no `tail_relevant` for the same reason they carry no `passage`: their whole served list is junk by label already. Between the stemmer block and the negatives sit the three DATE-SHAPED queries (GH #202): a query whose absent tokens are not words. A term the vault has never seen carries the MAXIMUM IDF, because "never seen" is the lexical half's strongest statement — right for a content word, and wrong for a year, a quarter, or a day, which a real vault query carries all the time and which no note need contain to be the answer. Neither existing bench could see the shape: no labelled query held one, and the title-as-query transfer bench is structurally blind to it, since a title's own tokens are in its own note by construction. Like the stemmer block, these deliberately BREAK the avoid-the-target's-keywords rule — the rule they exist to measure is lexical, so the query must have a lexical anchor to weigh the absent tokens against. They are graded on purpose: three absent numerics against four content words, then two against three, then one against several, so the bar is judged at more than one strength. The third is deliberately the dated twin of "recover a branch i deleted by accident" above — the same information need with a year in it, which is process rule 1's paired reading applied to a query shape rather than a config. Two-direction audit: each is anchored by a token unique to its labelled note (`hive`/`inspection` → week-log, `quarterly` → personal-finance, `reflog`/`deleted` → git-cheatsheet), and every numeric token (`2026`, `08`, `11`, `q1`, `2024`) reads zero occurrences corpus-wide, word-boundary and stem-prefix both.
